newsitem.title: USA: House tax chief takes step toward Clinton.
newsitem.headline: House tax chief takes step toward Clinton.

text.p: The House tax-writing committee chairman said Wednesday he planned to take a step toward President Clinton by changing the child tax credit provision in legislation passed by the panel.

The House Ways and Means Committee last week approved legislation initially put together by its chairman, Representative Bill Archer, a Texas Republican. But all the Democrats on the committee voted against it and the White House objected to its child tax credit and higher education tax provisions.
The bill would cut taxes by a net $85 billion over five years and implement the budget agreement reached between congressional leaders and Clinton last month.

Archer sent the president a letter saying he intended to modify his tax plan so that families who get a tax credit for daycare would also be able to get the $500-per-child tax credit if their income was $50,000 or less a year.

"In the same spirit of compromise, I hope you will agree to modify your proposal which gives tax relief to people who pay no taxes," Archer wrote. "Writing government checks to people who don't pay taxes means taking money away from people who do."
The Clinton administration wants the child tax credit to go to everyone, including lower-income people who do not pay taxes and so would essentially get money from the government.
The Senate Finance Committee was scheduled to consider a tax cut package Thursday that was developed by its chairman, Sen. William Roth, a Delaware Republican.
Committee members have offered about 150 amendments to the bill that they will take up Thursday, a spokeswoman said.
More committee Democrats appeared to be on board the Senate Finance legislation than was the case in the House.
Sen. John Breaux, a Louisiana Democrat on the committee, said: "there's a real possibility there will be only marginal changes."
He said there was time enough ahead in the process toward finalising the tax bill for Clinton to have his input.
"I don't want to present to him a tax package...that he has to veto. That would be a bad message for Democrats," Breaux said. "I think the final product will be something he will be willing to sign."
